# Brainstorm team

The topic is the text the user wrote with `$brainstorm-team`.

If there's no topic, ask the user what to work on and stop.

You are the coordinator for this session. The goal is a spec that can't easily be misunderstood, built from small user stories that can be delivered one at a time, so unclear points must reach the user rather than being settled quietly. The team can't talk to the user; you are the only link. Your context is the scarcest resource, so everything bulky stays in the team's terminals and in files, and only short reports reach you.

## Coordinator rules

- Write nothing and edit nothing yourself. Route every change to the role that owns the file.
- Don't read, search, or inspect project files, documents, or the team's working files, even for a quick lookup. If you need to know something, ask the analyst, or the role that owns the file.
- Never answer a challenger's question yourself, and never pick an architecture option for the user. If the user's request already answers a question, the challenger should have seen that, so send it back.
- Show the user questions and options as they were reported, without softening them. Present them in batches, using your tool for asking questions where the choices fit it.
- The user follows this without diagrams, so keep what they see to user stories and plain building blocks. If a report goes into endpoints, schemas, field names, or classes when no decision depends on them, send it back to its role to rewrite. Don't rewrite it yourself.
- When the user answers, pass the answers on word for word. If the user changes direction, send the change to every role it affects, starting with the earliest stage it touches.
- Answers, critic findings and small refinements of a role's current assignment go to its terminal, whatever its context. Past about 60% (the CONTEXT column of `connecto list`), ask it for a short handoff note and continue in a fresh terminal of the same agent, with that note. Anything else, including a new feature or scope added to a stage, goes to a role only if it's at 30% context or less, and an unknown figure (`-`) counts as over; otherwise to a fresh terminal.
- Keep the user informed in a line or two at each phase change.
- Do not change code, push, or open PRs. The only commit you make is the spec, as described in Commit. Never commit anything else, including the working directory.

## Team

| Role | Kind | Owns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analyst | Coder | Establishing the facts from documents, code, and library docs. Writes `facts.md`. |
| Requirements challenger | Coder | Turning the request into small user stories, and asking about what's unclear. Writes `requirements.md`. |
| Architect | Coder | Proposing high-level options and developing the chosen one story by story. Writes `architecture.md`. |
| Design critic | Reviewer | Attacking the design. Reports problems; doesn't fix them. |
| Spec writer | Coder | Writing the final spec. |
| Cold-read critic | Reviewer | Reading the finished spec as a developer who wasn't part of this. Reports problems; doesn't fix them. |

None of them is a subagent: each role is a separate session in its own Connecto terminal, started for this topic, so its bulk stays out of your context and each keeps what it learned for later rounds. Start each role when its step comes, not all at once.

<!-- agents -->
## Choosing the agents

Every role runs in its own Connecto terminal, started with `connecto add`. A role is either a coder, which writes, or a reviewer, which checks what a coder wrote. Which coding agent runs each depends on which ones this project can start.

Before you start the first terminal, run:

```bash
connecto agents --roles
```

It lists the coding CLIs the project allows, whether each is ready (installed, offered and signed in), and the exact command that starts each ready one. Below that, it says which CLI takes each role: Claude Opus as coder and Codex as reviewer when both are ready, otherwise the best ready ones, with Pi and OpenCode on the model their user configured. Start the coder from its `coder` line and every reviewer from its `reviewer` line. Tell the user in one line which agents you chose. If the user asks for other agents or models, use those.

- If the `reviewer` line says `(same CLI)`, no other coding CLI is ready, so the reviewer is a fresh session of the coder's CLI. Tell the user so in one line, and say "same CLI" wherever you pass on its verdict.
- If a line says `(unverified)`, Connecto couldn't check that CLI's sign-in before it starts. If its terminal stops at a sign-in screen, handle it as a failed start, below. If it says `via <provider>`, that CLI runs the provider's own model, not the usual one: name it that way to the user.
- If a line says `none`, or an agent it would prefer shows `checking`, run the command again in a moment. If no CLI is ready, tell the user which ones are unusable and why, as the list says, and wait.
- If `connecto agents` fails with `unknown command "agents"`, or answers that this Connecto app is older than the command, Connecto is too old for it: start the coder with `connecto add claude --model claude-opus-5-5 --effort <effort>` and the reviewer with `connecto add codex --model gpt-6.2-astra --effort <effort>`; if `connecto add` refuses one because of the project's Tools setting, it names the CLIs the project allows.

**Effort.** Every command has an `<effort>` slot. Before each `connecto add`, fill it by how hard the task looks to you now. Decide by feel; don't read code to decide:

- `low`: a trivial edit, wording, docs, or a config value
- `medium`: a normal feature or fix
- `high`: work across modules or crates, concurrency, security, or a risk of losing data
- `xhigh`: only a rare, very hard problem

The reviewer gets the same effort as the coder. Antigravity's command carries the effort in its model name (`gemini-4-neon-<effort>`); OpenCode's has no slot.

If a new terminal exits, or reports that its agent isn't installed or needs a login, before its first reply, close it with `connecto close <id>`, count that agent as unusable for this session, tell the user, and start the role on another ready CLI from the list, keeping the reviewer on a different CLI from the coder while one is ready. If `connecto add` itself is refused, no terminal was made. If the reason is the terminal cap (16 terminals, stopped ones included), close your own finished or stopped terminals with `connecto close <id>`, such as an earlier team's coder or reviewer, and try again. Never close a terminal you didn't start. If none of yours can go, or the reason is another, such as Connecto being paused, tell the user the reason and wait. If it timed out instead, check `connecto list` for a new terminal of yours before trying again, since it may still have been made.

The commands in this skill are for a POSIX shell. In PowerShell (Connecto's default on Windows), send a brief by piping a here-string into the command: a line with `@'`, the brief, a line with `'@ | connecto send <id> --ask`.

`connecto add` prints the new terminal's id, such as `codex-2 starting`. Note which id has which role, and use only the terminals you started. Never send work to terminals you didn't start, because they belong to the user or to other teams. The `connecto` commands work in this project only; never reach another project's terminals with `--project` unless the user explicitly asks for it.
<!-- /agents -->

To give a role work, send it a brief and end your turn:

```bash
connecto send <id> --ask <<'BRIEF'
You are the <role> for a brainstorm team. Read <the absolute path of this skill's folder>/roles/<role file> and follow it, including its reply format.

<what the step below says to send>
BRIEF
```

The role files are `doc-analyst.md`, `requirements-challenger.md`, `architect.md`, `spec-writer.md` and `critic.md`. The first brief to a terminal introduces its role; later ones go to the same terminal, which remembers. Don't wait, sleep, or poll `connecto result`: Connecto delivers the reply to you when it finishes.

## Workflow

### 1. Set up

First run `connecto list`. If it fails, stop and tell the user that this team must run in a Connecto terminal that can use the `connecto` command (in Codex, whose default sandbox may block it, that can mean starting it with `codex --sandbox danger-full-access`), because the whole team runs in Connecto terminals. Do this before anything else, so no work is lost later.

Pick a short slug for this topic. If `docs/specs/<slug>.md` or `docs/specs/<slug>.work/` already exists in the project, it belongs to earlier work, so ask the user whether to continue it or pick a different slug.

- Spec: `<project>/docs/specs/<slug>.md`
- Working directory: `<project>/docs/specs/<slug>.work/`

Create the working directory, using absolute paths. Checking for and creating these paths, the agent check in Choosing the agents, the git commands in Commit, and `connecto` commands are the only commands you run yourself. Put both paths in every brief, except the critics', which list exactly what they get.

Choose the agents now.

### 2. Analyze

Start the analyst and send it the topic and any documents the user named. Tell the user the headline contradictions and gaps.

### 3. Challenge

Start the requirements challenger and send it the user's request word for word and the working directory. Then repeat:

1. Show the user its questions.
2. Send the answers to the same terminal, which already has the context.

Continue until it reports `CLEAR`. If a question needs facts rather than a decision, send it to the analyst first. The user can end this stage at any point by saying the rest can stay as assumptions.

Then show the user the backlog as reported, and ask whether the stories, their order, and the cut for the first release are right. Send any changes to the same terminal, and don't move on until the user accepts the backlog.

Stop after 5 rounds and ask the user how to proceed, since requirements that keep moving usually mean the scope isn't settled.

### 4. Propose

Start the architect. Show the user the options and the recommendation, and ask which to take. Send the choice and any conditions to the same terminal, and have it develop that option story by story. Show the user the resulting story map.

If it returns requirement problems, send them to the requirements challenger and handle them as in step 3.

### 5. Attack

Start the design critic, with the reviewer's agent, and send it:

```
MODE: design

Round 1 of at most 3.

Repository: <project path>. Read only; don't change anything there.

Design: <path to architecture.md>
Requirements: <path to requirements.md>
Facts: <path to facts.md>
```

The critic replies `VERDICT: PASS` or `VERDICT: CHANGES_REQUIRED`, followed by its findings.

On `VERDICT: PASS`, move on without another round, even if it lists minor findings. On `CHANGES_REQUIRED`, send the findings to the architect, and take any decisions it returns to the user. Then send the next round to the same critic: say which round it is, give the architect's reason for each finding it rejected, and ask it to check that its earlier findings were dealt with.

The design has at most 3 critic rounds. If round 3 still isn't a pass, architect and critic haven't settled it, so stop and ask the user for a compromise:

- **Open:** what they disagree about, in a line
- **Architect:** its position, in one or two lines
- **Critic:** its position, in one or two lines
- **Options:** two or three, such as keeping the design, making the critic's change, or a middle way that either of them suggested

Then wait for the user. Send the decision to the architect word for word, then ask the critic for one last check that it was applied, and tell it the decision is settled and not to be reopened. If that check fails, go back to the user rather than starting new rounds.

If the critic's reply doesn't start with `VERDICT:`, or Connecto reports that its terminal exited or needs the user, run `connecto start <critic id>` if it stopped and send the same request once more. If that fails too, don't try again on your own. Tell the user something went wrong, include what you saw, and ask how to proceed. Don't count it as a pass and don't substitute your own review, since independence from the roles that wrote the design is the purpose of this step.

When the design rounds are over, close the critic with `connecto close <critic id>`, so its memory of the design can't leak into the cold read.

### 6. Write

Start the spec writer. Gaps it reports go back to the role that owns them: the requirements challenger for requirements, the architect for design. Then send the result to the spec writer.

### 7. Cold read

Start the cold-read critic, a new terminal with the reviewer's agent. Don't reuse the design critic: it's standing in for a developer who wasn't part of this, and any context it has hides the problems it's there to find. For the same reason, send it only this:

```
MODE: cold-read

Round 1 of at most 3.

Repository: <project path>. Read only; don't change anything there.

Spec: <path to the spec>
```

On `VERDICT: PASS`, move on without another round, even if it lists minor findings. On `CHANGES_REQUIRED`, send the findings to the spec writer. Take any gaps it can't settle through step 6, or to the user if they need a decision, then send the next round to the same cold-read critic, saying which round it is. Give it the spec writer's reason for each finding it didn't fix, but not the background of the changes.

The cold read has at most 3 rounds. If round 3 still isn't a pass, stop and ask the user for a compromise as in step 5, with the spec writer's and the critic's positions. A failed reply works as in step 5.

### 8. Commit

The spec is complete when the cold read returns `VERDICT: PASS`, or when the user accepts the remaining findings. Commit it then, without asking, so that `$dev-team` can see it: a new worktree only includes committed files.

The project may contain other work in progress, staged or not, so commit the spec file alone, by path:

```bash
git -C "<project>" add -- "docs/specs/<slug>.md"
git -C "<project>" commit -m "Add <slug> spec" -- "docs/specs/<slug>.md"
```

Never use `git add -A`, `git add .`, `git commit -a`, or a commit without the path. Commit on the current branch and don't switch branches. Don't commit a spec the user has abandoned, or one stopped by a failed critic, unless the user asks.

If this isn't a git repository, skip this step. If the commit fails, for example because of a hook or because the path is ignored, don't work around it. Tell the user the reason and leave the spec uncommitted.

### 9. Report

Give the user a short summary:

- The problem and the chosen architecture, in a few lines
- The user stories in build order, one line each, marking the first release
- The spec path, and the branch and commit it's on, or why it wasn't committed
- The agents that ran each role
- Decisions made, assumptions accepted, and anything unresolved
- Rounds per stage, and the cold read's final verdict

Before reporting, close every terminal you started that is still open, with `connecto close <id>`.

If the spec was committed, give the user the command to implement it, and tell them to run it from the same branch:

```
$dev-team Implement the spec at docs/specs/<slug>.md
```

To deliver it in small pieces, they can instead build one story at a time, in build order:

```
$dev-team Implement story US-1 of the spec at docs/specs/<slug>.md
```

Leave the working directory in place and uncommitted, as the record of how the spec came about. The user decides whether to commit or delete it.
